puzzles.title: One reading, one day
puzzles.question: Use the training days in station_ledger. Fit a logistic regression model that predicts eruption_within_week from tremor_level alone, then run predictWithModel() on the training days. What probability_yes does the model give the day 2014-07-15?
puzzles.starter_code:
training_days <- station_ledger %>%
  filter(record == "training")

model <- buildModel(
  data = training_days,
  model_type = "logistic_regression",
  predictors = "____",
  response = "eruption_within_week"
)
puzzles.solution:
training_days <- station_ledger %>%
  filter(record == "training")

model <- buildModel(
  data = training_days,
  model_type = "logistic_regression",
  predictors = "tremor_level",
  response = "eruption_within_week"
)

predictWithModel(data = training_days, model = model) %>%
  filter(date == "2014-07-15") %>%
  select(date, tremor_level, probability_yes)
puzzles.right_feedback: Right: the tremor_level model gives 2014-07-15 that probability of an eruption within the week.
puzzles.wrong_feedback: Not that one. Check the model uses tremor_level alone and the training days only, then filter the predictions to the date 2014-07-15 and read probability_yes.

puzzles.title: Calls on the held-back days
puzzles.question: Use station_ledger. Fit a logistic regression model on the training days with the predictors gas_ratio, sulfur_dioxide_tonnes_per_day, vent_temperature_c and air_temperature_c (response eruption_within_week), then predict the held-back days with predictWithModel(). At the 0.5 cut-off, on how many held-back days does the model say yes (predicted_class is yes)?
puzzles.starter_code:
training_days <- station_ledger %>%
  filter(record == "training")
held_back_days <- station_ledger %>%
  filter(record == "held back")
puzzles.solution:
training_days <- station_ledger %>%
  filter(record == "training")
held_back_days <- station_ledger %>%
  filter(record == "held back")

model <- buildModel(
  data = training_days,
  model_type = "logistic_regression",
  predictors = c("gas_ratio", "sulfur_dioxide_tonnes_per_day", "vent_temperature_c", "air_temperature_c"),
  response = "eruption_within_week"
)

predictions <- predictWithModel(data = held_back_days, model = model)

predictions %>%
  summarize(called_yes = sum(predicted_class == "yes"))
puzzles.right_feedback: Right: that is how many held-back days the model calls yes at the 0.5 cut-off.
puzzles.wrong_feedback: Not that one. Check the predictors are gas_ratio, sulfur_dioxide_tonnes_per_day, vent_temperature_c and air_temperature_c, the model is fitted on the training days, and you count predicted_class == "yes" on the held-back days.

puzzles.title: Caught and missed
puzzles.question: Use station_ledger. Fit a logistic regression model on the training days with the predictors tremor_level and sulfur_dioxide_tonnes_per_day (response eruption_within_week), then predict the held-back days with predictWithModel(). Of the held-back days followed by an eruption within the week (eruption_within_week is yes), on how many did the model say yes (caught), and on how many did it say no (missed)?
puzzles.starter_code:
training_days <- station_ledger %>%
  filter(record == "training")
held_back_days <- station_ledger %>%
  filter(record == "held back")
puzzles.solution:
training_days <- station_ledger %>%
  filter(record == "training")
held_back_days <- station_ledger %>%
  filter(record == "held back")

model <- buildModel(
  data = training_days,
  model_type = "logistic_regression",
  predictors = c("tremor_level", "sulfur_dioxide_tonnes_per_day"),
  response = "eruption_within_week"
)

predictions <- predictWithModel(data = held_back_days, model = model)

predictions %>%
  filter(eruption_within_week == "yes") %>%
  summarize(caught = sum(predicted_class == "yes"),
            missed = sum(predicted_class == "no"))
puzzles.right_feedback: Right: caught and missed together are every held-back eruption day.
puzzles.wrong_feedback: Not that one. Keep only the held-back days where eruption_within_week is yes, then count predicted_class yes (caught) and no (missed).

puzzles.title: Which predictor weighs most?
puzzles.question: Use the training plates in survey_plates. Scale color_index, axis_ratio and apparent_size_arcsec, fit a logistic regression model that predicts elliptical from all three, and look at the three coefficients. Which predictor has the largest scaled coefficient, ignoring its sign?
puzzles.starter_code:
training_plates <- survey_plates %>%
  filter(record == "training")

scaled_plates <- training_plates %>%
  mutate(across(c(____, ____, ____), scale))
puzzles.solution:
training_plates <- survey_plates %>%
  filter(record == "training")

scaled_plates <- training_plates %>%
  mutate(across(c(color_index, axis_ratio, apparent_size_arcsec), scale))

model <- buildModel(
  data = scaled_plates,
  model_type = "logistic_regression",
  predictors = c("color_index", "axis_ratio", "apparent_size_arcsec"),
  response = "elliptical"
)

model$metrics %>%
  filter(type == "coefficient")
puzzles.right_feedback: Right: once all three are scaled, its coefficient is the largest in size.
puzzles.wrong_feedback: Not that one. Scale color_index, axis_ratio and apparent_size_arcsec first, fit on the scaled training plates, and compare the size of the coefficients (not the intercept), ignoring the sign.

puzzles.title: The model or calling everything a spiral?
puzzles.question: Use survey_plates. Fit a logistic regression model on the training plates with the predictors concentration, axis_ratio and apparent_size_arcsec (response elliptical), then predict the held-back plates with predictWithModel(). Compare its accuracy with calling every held-back galaxy a spiral (always "no"). Which is more accurate, and how many of the held-back ellipticals does the model catch? (Calling everything a spiral catches none.)
puzzles.starter_code:
training_plates <- survey_plates %>%
  filter(record == "training")
held_back_plates <- survey_plates %>%
  filter(record == "held back")
puzzles.solution:
training_plates <- survey_plates %>%
  filter(record == "training")
held_back_plates <- survey_plates %>%
  filter(record == "held back")

model <- buildModel(
  data = training_plates,
  model_type = "logistic_regression",
  predictors = c("concentration", "axis_ratio", "apparent_size_arcsec"),
  response = "elliptical"
)

predictions <- predictWithModel(data = held_back_plates, model = model)

predictions %>%
  summarize(model_accuracy = mean(predicted_class == elliptical),
            all_spiral_accuracy = mean(elliptical == "no"),
            model_catches = sum(predicted_class == "yes" & elliptical == "yes"))

puzzles.title: The model or calling everything a spiral?
puzzles.question: Use survey_plates. Fit a logistic regression model on the training plates with the predictors axis_ratio, apparent_size_arcsec and exposure_minutes (response elliptical), then predict the held-back plates with predictWithModel(). Compare its accuracy with calling every held-back galaxy a spiral (always "no"). Which is more accurate, and how many of the held-back ellipticals does the model catch? (Calling everything a spiral catches none.)
puzzles.starter_code:
training_plates <- survey_plates %>%
  filter(record == "training")
held_back_plates <- survey_plates %>%
  filter(record == "held back")
puzzles.solution:
training_plates <- survey_plates %>%
  filter(record == "training")
held_back_plates <- survey_plates %>%
  filter(record == "held back")

model <- buildModel(
  data = training_plates,
  model_type = "logistic_regression",
  predictors = c("axis_ratio", "apparent_size_arcsec", "exposure_minutes"),
  response = "elliptical"
)

predictions <- predictWithModel(data = held_back_plates, model = model)

predictions %>%
  summarize(model_accuracy = mean(predicted_class == elliptical),
            all_spiral_accuracy = mean(elliptical == "no"),
            model_catches = sum(predicted_class == "yes" & elliptical == "yes"))
